fact_en: A bulb has a flat base where roots grow downward, while leaves sprout upward from the top.
fact_bis: Ang bombilya adunay patag nga bahin sa ilalom diin motubo paubos ang mga gamot, ug sa ibabaw motubo pataas ang mga dahon.

findings.note: Plant bulb rendered 'bombilya', which in Cebuano means an electric light bulb. The card then says roots grow down from its flat base and leaves grow up — a child reads that a light bulb grows roots and leaves. Nothing in the card (title_bis is only 'Gamot Paubos Dahon Pataas') names the plant structure, so the actual subject is unrecoverable. Correct sense would be the onion/garlic-type bulb (e.g. 'bonggolan'/'ang bulb sa tanom sama sa sibuyas').

fact_en: Remove a bee stinger by scraping it sideways with a card — this stops the venom sac from pumping more poison into your skin.
fact_bis: Kuhaa ang tibo sa buyog pinaagi sa pag-scrape niini sa kilid gamit ang card — para dili na makapump ang venom sac og dugang hilo sa imong panit.

findings.note: title_bis 'Gasgas sa Card sa Tuko' — 'tuko' is a gecko in Cebuano, not a stinger. English title is 'Scrape Out the Stinger'; the body correctly uses 'tibo sa buyog' (bee stinger), so the title names an animal that has nothing to do with the card (likely a mangling of 'tusok'/'tibo').

fact_en: Before the itchy chickenpox blisters even appear, a child usually already has a fever and body aches.
fact_bis: Sa dili pa motungha ang mga butlig sa bulutong-tubig, ang bata kasagaran naa na'y hilanat ug labad sa lawas.

findings.note: title_bis 'Bakuna nga Hilanat ug Rash' says VACCINE (bakuna) causes the fever and rash. The card is about chickenpox (bulutong-tubig) causing fever before the blisters — no vaccine is involved. Title-level defect with a health-misinformation reading ('vaccines give you fever and rash'); body uses 'bulutong-tubig' correctly, but the title as displayed names the wrong thing.

fact_en: The pangolin has an amazingly long, sticky tongue that it uses to catch ants and termites hiding underground.
fact_bis: Ang pangolin adunay hataas kaayo ug malapot nga dila nga gigamit niini sa pagdakop og langgam ug termite ilawom sa yuta.

findings.note: 'ants' translated as 'langgam', which in Cebuano means BIRD (the Tagalog false friend: TL langgam = ant, CEB langgam = bird). Card says the pangolin's sticky tongue catches 'langgam ug termite ilawom sa yuta' — birds and termites underground. The card never restores 'ants' (Cebuano 'hulmigas'), and elsewhere in this same corpus 'langgam' is used correctly for birds, so the child has no way to recover the fact.

fact_en:
What's the largest living thing on Earth?

It's a honey fungus in Oregon, USA — its underground network covers more than 2,300 acres of forest, making it the largest living organism on Earth.
fact_bis:
Unsa ang pinakadako nga buhi nga butang sa kalibutan?

Usa ka honey fungus sa Oregon, USA — ang ilawom-yuta nga network niini nagtabon og kapin 2,300 ka ektarya sa kagubatan, mao nga kini ang pinakadako nga buhing organismo sa kalibutan.

findings.note: Unit changed: English '2,300 acres' becomes '2,300 ka ektarya' (hectares). 2,300 acres is about 930 hectares, so the Cebuano overstates the honey fungus's area by ~2.5x. Number-with-unit is the whole point of the card and is not corrected anywhere.

fact_en: Vines, also called lianas, climb up rainforest trees to reach the sunlight high in the canopy.
fact_bis: Ang mga gapnod o liana mokatay paibabaw sa mga kahoy aron maabot ang kahayag sa canopy.

findings.note: Body opens "Ang mga gapnod o liana mokatay paibabaw sa mga kahoy" — `gapnod` is driftwood/water-borne debris, not a vine (Cebuano is `balagon`, or `baging`). The card names a different thing as its lead noun and `gapnod` is also seeded into `terms` alongside `baging`, so retrieval carries the bad pairing too. Partial mitigation: title_bis is correctly "Mga Baging" and `liana` is kept in-line, so the climbing-for-canopy-light fact itself survives — flagging mainly because the wrong-word pair is corpus-wide greppable and was written into terms on purpose.

fact_en: When a millipede feels threatened, it coils into a tight spiral to protect the soft underside of its body.
fact_bis: Kon mobati'g kapeligrohan ang millipede, maglikit kini pag-ayo nga morag spiral aron panalipdan ang humok nga ubos sa iyang lawas.

findings.note: title_bis 'Pagliko sa Alupihan' names the centipede, but the card is about a millipede coiling into a spiral. The corpus consistently uses 'alupihan' for centipede and leaves millipede in English (ffct-01041 contrasts 'millipede ug alupihan'; ffct-09946 'Ang alupihan adunay usa ka paris nga tiil sa matag segment'). The Cebuano body never supplies a Cebuano name, so the title is uncorrected and teaches that a centipede is the animal that curls up - the exact trait that separates millipedes from centipedes.

fact_en: There is a special joint in front of your ear that moves your jaw up, down, and sideways so you can chew food and speak.
fact_bis: Adunay lutahan sa atubangan sa dalunggan nga nagpalihok sa apapangig paibabaw, paubos, ug sa kilid aron makakaon ug makasulti ka.

findings.note: title_bis "Sakit sa Baba" (mouth pain/illness) for title_en "Jaw Joint Chewing". The card is pure anatomy — a joint in front of the ear that moves the apapangig up, down and sideways so you can chew and speak — and never mentions pain or disease. Using "Baba" for jaw is a corpus title convention (ffct-14407 "Molars sa Baba", ffct-14495 "Honey Badger sa Baba"), so the defect is "Sakit": all 25 other "Sakit ..." titles in the corpus sit on English titles that really are about pain or disease, making this one the lone outlier that renames the card's topic.

fact_en: The stem of kangkong is hollow inside — that's exactly what lets it float on top of the water.
fact_bis: Ang punoan sa kangkong hungkag sa sulod — mao nga makalutaw kini sa ibabaw sa tubig.

findings.note: title_bis "Lihog sa Kangkong" for "Kangkong Stems". Lihog/palihog means please/a favour, not stem; the body correctly uses "punoan". Same wrong mapping recurs corpus-wide in exactly the stem slot — ffct-01646 "Tubig sa Lihog" (Water in Stems) and ffct-37862 "Gibag-on sa Lihog" (Stem Thickness) — so it is one lexicon entry, not a typo, and a single fix covers 3 titles. Title-only; the body of each card still delivers the fact, so treat as lower severity than the two above.

fact_en:
Why does your tummy rumble when you're hungry?

When your stomach is empty, it releases a chemical that tells your brain it's time to eat — that's why your tummy rumbles and you start thinking about food!
fact_bis:
Nganong magkalibang ang tiyan kon gutom?

Kon walay sulod ang tiyan, mopagawas kini og kemikal nga magsulti sa utok nga oras na para mokaon — mao nga magkalibang ang tiyan ug maghunahuna ta og pagkaon!

findings.note: EN: "Why does your tummy rumble when you're hungry?" BIS renders rumble as "magkalibang" twice: "Nganong magkalibang ang tiyan kon gutom?" ... "mao nga magkalibang ang tiyan". In this corpus kalibang always means defecate/diarrhea (58 hits, e.g. ffct-00355 "Kon ang bata magkalibang o magsuka", ffct-02996 "Rason sa Kalibang"). Every other stomach-growl card uses mosaba / mongulob / mokuros / mokabog / nagpakagol (ffct-04401, ffct-11180, ffct-14596, ffct-12944). A Cebuano-only child reads that an empty stomach makes you move your bowels; the rumbling-sound fact is never delivered anywhere on the card.

fact_en: Water birds like ducks have webbed feet — skin stretched between their toes — that help them paddle through water.
fact_bis: Ang mga langgam sa tubig sama sa itik adunay tiil nga may lapyahan tali sa mga tudlo, nga makatabang kanila nga mogaud sa tubig.

findings.note: title_bis "Tiil nga Lambay" for EN title "Webbed Feet". `lambay` is the swimming crab in Cebuano — elsewhere in this same corpus it is used exactly that way ("Ang kugita mokaon og lambay, pasayan, ug kinhason"). The title therefore reads "crab feet" on a card about ducks. The body does give the right term ("tiil nga may lapyahan tali sa mga tudlo"), so this is a title-only defect, flagged because it names a different animal in the title.

fact_en: Your teeth have different jobs: sharp incisors up front for cutting, pointy canines for tearing, and flat premolars and molars in back for crushing and grinding.
fact_bis: Ang imong mga ngipon adunay lain-laing trabaho: hait nga incisors sa atubangan para moputol, hait nga canines para mopunit, ug patag nga premolars ug molars sa luyo para modugmok ug mongab-ok.

findings.note: Types-of-teeth card. EN: "pointy canines for tearing". BIS: "hait nga canines para mopunit" — `punit` is to pick up / gather (corpus-wide it is used only that way: "pagpunit ug basura", "napunit nga palay", "mopunit og bato"), not to tear (`mogisi`). The card lists one job per tooth type (cut / tear / crush-grind) and nothing else in the Cebuano restores tearing, so a child reading only the Cebuano learns canines are for picking things up.
